cards.text: This song comes from Asaph, the Levite David made chief of the worship music (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). He opens with a prayer to God. No warm-up, no small talk, friend. He goes STRAIGHT to it.

cards.question: Asaph opens by asking God the same thing three different ways. What is he asking God not to be?

cards.text: Then Asaph points God to what's going on: "See how Your enemies rage, how Your foes have reared their heads."

cards.question: These raging enemies scheme with cunning. Asaph says they're plotting against God's ___.
The enemies have a plan, and Asaph quotes it. What do they say they want to do to Israel?

cards.text: "Come, let us erase them as a nation; may the name of Israel be remembered no more." Friend, I spent YEARS forgotten in the back of a junk drawer, and nobody was working THAT hard at it.

cards.question: Asaph says the nations plotting against Israel can't agree on a plan.
These nations plot together with one mind and form an alliance. Who does Asaph say the alliance is against?

cards.text: Then Asaph names ten who are in on it, from Edom, Moab and Ammon to Philistia and Tyre, all the way to Assyria, lending strength to the sons of Lot. That's not an alliance, friend. That's a GROUP CHAT, and there's only one topic.

Asaph's got a whole crowd lined up against God's people, so he pulls out the receipts, OLD ones: Midian, and Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon. Midian is the nation God once handed Israel over to for seven years (Judges 6:1), and Sisera was commander of King Jabin's army (Judges 4:2).

cards.question: Asaph brings up Midian, Sisera and Jabin. What is he asking God to do to today's enemies?

answers.text: Defeat them like He defeated those enemies
Send them back to their own lands

cards.text: Asaph does NOT soften it, friend: they perished at Endor and became like dung on the ground. Then he asks God to make today's nobles and princes like four leaders of Midian: Oreb and Zeeb (Judges 7:25), Zebah and Zalmunna (Judges 8:5).

cards.question: Asaph quotes a boast from those old Midian leaders, like Zebah and Zalmunna. What did they want to possess for themselves?

cards.text: Then Asaph trades the history lesson for pictures: "Make them like tumbleweed, O my God, like chaff before the wind."

cards.question: Tumbleweed and chaff before the wind. Asaph is asking God to make the enemies easy to ___ away.

cards.text: Like crumbs on my counter when I blow on them. FWOOSH. Gone. Then the next picture: fire eating up a forest, and a flame setting the mountains ablaze.

cards.question: After the fire picture, Asaph asks God to chase the enemies down with a flood.

cards.text: No flood. Just like fire sweeping the mountains, Asaph says, "so pursue them with Your tempest, and terrify them with Your storm."
Then the prayer takes a turn I did NOT see coming. Asaph asks God to cover their faces with shame, and he says what it's for.

cards.question: Asaph asks God to cover the enemies' faces with shame. Why?

answers.text: So they may seek the LORD's name
So Israel can laugh at them

cards.question: After praying that the enemies seek the LORD's name, Asaph stops asking for them to be ashamed.

cards.text: Next line: "May they be ever ashamed and terrified; may they perish in disgrace." Then comes his very last line, and it's about what he wants them to know.

cards.question: Asaph ends his prayer with what he wants the enemies to know. What is it?

answers.text: That the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth
That Israel will rule over every nation on earth
That Asaph's prayers are always heard in heaven

findings.problem: The opening card has four sentences: 'This song comes from Asaph...', 'He opens with a prayer to God.', 'No warm-up, no small talk, friend.' and 'He goes STRAIGHT to it.'

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: The card is only a lead-in plus the verse quote. It has no Papa Dorin voice or reaction, so it reads as a bare reading of Psalm 83:2.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The story card has three sentences: the list of nations, 'That's not an alliance, friend.' and 'That's a GROUP CHAT, and there's only one topic.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This is the setup for card 2, which asks what Asaph wants God to do to the enemies (defeat them as before). The only extra context given points the other way. It says Midian is the nation God handed Israel over to (Judges 6:1) and that Sisera commanded Jabin's army. Nothing says these enemies were defeated, so the baker has no basis for reasoning to 'Defeat them like He defeated those enemies.'

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The card says the boast in Psalm 83:12 came from 'those old Midian leaders, like Zebah and Zalmunna.' In the text, 'who said' could point back to Zebah and Zalmunna or to the present enemies' nobles and princes, and the text leaves it open. The card also calls the line a 'boast' when the text only says 'who said.'

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The story card has four sentences: 'Like crumbs on my counter when I blow on them.', 'FWOOSH.', 'Gone.' and 'Then the next picture...'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card uses verse 14's picture ('Just like fire sweeping the mountains') to frame verse 15, but it cites only Psalm 83:15. It should cite Psalm 83:14-15.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The card tells verse 18's content ('his very last line... it's about what he wants them to know,' from 'May they know') but cites only Psalm 83:17. It should cite Psalm 83:17-18.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: 'Next line:' plus a verse quote and a lead-in. There is no Papa Dorin voice or reaction on the card.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
